newsitem.title: USA: NCAA BASKETBALL-ARIZONA, KENTUCKY SUCCEED WITHOUT CLASSIC CENTERS.
newsitem.headline: NCAA BASKETBALL-ARIZONA, KENTUCKY SUCCEED WITHOUT CLASSIC CENTERS.

text.p: In addition to a nickname, the Kentucky and Arizona Wildcats share this: both teams head into Monday night's college basketball championship game without a classic, seven-foot (2.13 meters) centre.

Last year's NBA finalists, the Chicago Bulls and Seattle SuperSonics also had no dominant pivot men, and some coaches have been saying for a while now that the trend in basketball is towards the more athletic, "swingman" player.

Arizona coach Lute Olson quotes legendary UCLA coach John Wooden, creator of college basketball's greatest dynasty, as saying: "Give me the quickest player that you can give me, because quickness will outdo size any day of the week."
Of course, Wooden also coached Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Bill Walton, two of the greatest centres ever.
"I think the game has really changed," said Olson.
"I think the days of the 7 foot, 7-1, 7-2, 6-11 (2.13, 2.16, 2.18, 2.11 meters) slow guys, I think those days are numbered.
"Right now I think the toughest people to contend with are the 6-9, 6-8, 6-7 (2.06, 2.03, 2.01 meters) athletes, because they don't restrict what you do offensively.

"Kentucky creates tremendous problems for us and for other teams because you've got to defend all five of their guys out at the three-point line. You can't sit somebody in the middle of the lane and make them come to you. So I think that's a wave of the future, because of the three-point line."

Kentucky coach Rick Pitino agrees on the value of the versatile player who can score from outside the three-point line or drive to the basket, where he can score or draw fouls. And he sees on the Arizona squad some prime examples of such hard-to-guard players.

"If you have people that just spot up from the three, then you can take it away. When you have people the way they handle it and go to the (foul) line 37 times per game, what they do is what all three-point attacks do, they look to get the three or the easy shot in the lane," said Pitino.

The Kentucky coach said his players were able to key on just a couple offensive threats in beating Minnesota Saturday night, and North Carolina, with its big front line, also was limited against Arizona in their semifinal.

"When you look out there like last night, and same thing for the North Carolina game, any time you can devise your system to play five versus three or five versus four by going off nonshooters or people that aren't as quick, you have an edge defensively.
"That's why quickness and shooting is so important," said Pitino, a former head coach of the NBA's New York Knicks.

"When you're looking at Arizona, you can't devise your system, because they shoot the ball so well in so many different positions and handle it. You know, players that can pass, catch, put it on the floor and shoot, it's a rare quality today.
"And that's what you have to look for, and Arizona has done a wonderful job of rtecruiting players like that. I think we've done a very good job of recruiting players like that."
Certainly the Arizona players are proud of their speed.
"I don't think you'll find any faster big men," said 6-8 (2.03 meters) Bennett Davison.
"At Arizona everyone is athletic. We can run and jump. Everyone has quickness and Coach built the team around that."
"Our big men like to run the floor and theirs do, too," said Arizona's 6-11 (2.11 meters) A.J. Bramlett. "It matches both teams' strengths."
"This is a team that goes to all their players," Pitino said of Arizona, noting that Olson's crew also knocked off top-ranked Kansas despite a supposed height disadvantage.
"They've got incredible quickness and speed, and they didn't beat Kansas on a fluke game. They beat Kansas because they were outstanding against an outstanding ball club."
Pitino says his players are not quite as quick as Arizona's in the "4 and 5 spots" -- the traditional power forward and power forward spots.

But he claims to have "the best player in the country" in the graceful, 6-7 (2.01 meters) guard/forward Ron Mercer, who has already said he will enter the NBA draft this year after just two seasons of college ball. Pitino lost four players from last year's championship team to the pros.

"We try to recruit a certain type of basketball player that fits our needs," said Pitino. "He has to be able to run, catch, shoot, have that potential. And we've obviously had some great players who have gone on to have some outstanding pro careers early on.
"Right now we know Ron is going to be able to do that."
